title: Senior's toolkit: logs and text
summary: tail -F, less, grep, awk, sort, sed, jq and xargs: answer questions from logs in one pipeline.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: logs and text
steps.body: Most incidents are answered by a pipeline over a log file. These are the pieces people chain together without looking anything up.

toolkit.what: Follows a log as it grows and keeps following when logrotate replaces the file. Plain `-f` silently stops at rotation.
flags: follow by name, reopen after rotation

toolkit.what: Opens a big file without loading it all. `+F` follows like tail; Ctrl+C stops following so you can search, `F` resumes.
flags: search, next, previous, jump to end

toolkit.what: Finds matching lines with context. Combine `-v`, `-c` and `-o` to filter, count or extract.
The "top N" pipeline: pick a column, count each value, biggest first. Works for status codes, IPs, paths, users.
flags: the ninth space-separated field (the status in nginx's default log)
count runs of equal lines (so sort first)
toolkit.example: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

toolkit.what: Sorts by one column. `-k3,3` means "only column 3"; `-k3` alone means "from column 3 to the end".
Edits a file in place with a regex, keeping a backup. The standard one-line config change in a script.
flags: edit in place, save the original as `.bak`

toolkit.what: Filters and reshapes JSON: structured logs, API responses, `kubectl -o json`.
flags: pass a shell value in safely

toolkit.what: Runs a command over many files safely (spaces in names) and in parallel.
flags: separate names with NUL, not spaces

steps.prompt: You left `tail -f /var/log/app.log` running overnight. The app is clearly still logging, but no new lines have appeared since 00:00. Why?
options: logrotate renamed the file at midnight and `-f` kept following the old one; use `tail -F`
The app now logs to the journal
steps.explain: `-f` follows the open file descriptor, which now points at `app.log.1`. `-F` follows the name and reopens it when a new file appears.

steps.prompt: Count the HTTP status codes in an nginx access log, most common first.
steps.code: awk '{print $__1__}' access.log | sort | uniq -__2__ | sort -__3__ | head
steps.explain: In the default combined format the status is field 9 (`$1` is the client IP). `uniq -c` counts adjacent equal lines, which is why the first `sort` is needed. `sort -rn` puts the largest count first.
`-t,` splits on commas and `-k2,2n` sorts by the second column as a number: 2, 3, 10. Without `n` it would sort as text, and `10` would come first.

steps.prompt: Match each jq filter to what it gives you.
pairs: the token without quotes, for a shell variable

steps.prompt: Which tool is the right one for the job?
items: The fourth column of a space-separated log
Sum the bytes column of an access log
The `msg` field of every error in a JSON log
Pod names from `kubectl get pods -o json`

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When someone asks "how many", "which one most" or "since when" about a log, answer with a pipeline instead of scrolling. Build it one stage at a time with `| head` at the end, then keep the good ones in your notes: you will need them again at 3 a.m.
